extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/history of science and scientific method (readers of Bacon/Inductive Logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply normative criteria for good vs. bad methods of scientific inquiry as discussed in Bacon's Novum Organum and the commentary: what practices advance knowledge and what practices obstruct it. Focuses on ordering of experience, authority, experiment, and avoidance of superstition/vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge referred to use and action
rubrics_metrics.description: All knowledge should be referred to use and action (Bacon's stated maxim: 'All knowledge should be referred to use and action').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records Bacon's view ('All knowledge should be referred to use and action') and also offers a critique: that taking an unduly narrow view of knowledge-as-instrumental risks ignoring legitimate intellectual pleasures and the elevating influence of pure investigation. Use this criterion to evaluate claims that knowledge must be justified solely by practical utility; consider also non-instrumental values (intellectual pleasure, diversion from selfish aims, widening of intellect and character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forming conclusions by collecting opinions/authorities alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the method of merely collecting opinions and authorities and, by comparing and reflecting on them, attempting to arrive at an opinion of one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is identified in the text as one of the 'false methods' of enquiry: assembling authorities without testing their foundations leads only to revolving in opinions. Use this to flag approaches that substitute citation/appeal-to-authority for empirical investigation or critical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dialectical/syllogistic method without examining foundational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject reliance on the dialectical (syllogistical) method that takes first principles for granted (often borrowed from professors) and pursues consequences without enquiring into the truth of the data on which they are based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary criticises using dialectic to invent only what seems consistent with assumed principles, rather than testing or re-examining those principles. Evaluate methods that build elaborate theoretical deductions without checking their empirical premises; prioritize verification of first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unguided experience ('experientia mera')
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience consulted 'without any definite order or method' ('experientia mera')—mere casual or random experimentation—is inadequate for discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text likens unguided experience to 'palpation' in the dark: it may sometimes stumble upon results by chance but is inferior. Use this to criticise experimental programs lacking systematic design, controls, or a plan for generalisation; demand organized, repeatable, and directed experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order experience and derive axioms from it (true empirical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true order of experience lights a lamp first and then shows the way: begin with ordered and digested experience (not preposterous or erratic), derive axioms from it, and from axioms produce new experiments and further knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This positive methodological criterion prescribes: (a) begin with well-ordered observations/experiments, (b) extract general axioms from them, and (c) return to experiment guided by those axioms. Use to evaluate whether an investigation is iterative, systematic, and builds generalizable principles rather than relying on chance or deduction alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give undue reverence to antiquity, authority, or consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive respect for antiquity and authority (the commentary: 'Veritas Temporis filia, non Authoritatis' — truth is daughter of time, not of authority); reverence for ancient authors or consensus can arrest progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents how deference to ancient authorities causes people to persist in error. Apply this criterion to work that unquestioningly privileges canonical texts or consensus over new evidence; encourage skepticism of authority and evaluation based on contemporary data and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware admiration of finished works and apparatus distracting from primary observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration of mechanical arts, elaborate apparatus, and the products of craftsmanship can incline minds toward admiration of human opulence rather than attention to primitive observations and natural operations (the 'primitivas hominis observationes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to critique research that is seduced by complexity, instrumentation, or polished artifacts at the expense of attending to simple, primary phenomena and first principles. Check that novelty/complexity is grounded in explanatory observational bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute library study for experimental investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting from workshops to libraries and admiring vast varieties of books can induce stupefaction: libraries often contain endless repetition and do not substitute for fresh experimental inquiry ('nullum dari finem repetitionibus... eadem agant et loquantur').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this when work relies primarily on literature survey or citation-network reinforcement without complementary empirical work. Libraries inform but cannot replace ordered experimental investigation; beware endless commentary that produces no new observation or experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of impostors, alchemists, and superstitious claims promising miraculous results
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who promise extravagant benefits (long life, transmutations, occult revelations, miraculous operations) have burdened human progress with vain hopes; while some alchemists found useful things, overall such pursuits encouraged error, repetition, and distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard to demand evidence for extraordinary claims and to penalize work that relies on occult, unrepeatable, or plausibly fraudulent practices. Accept that some practitioners in marginal traditions produced useful results, but require rigorous reproducibility and reject appeals to miracle or tradition to justify claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer appropriate methodological form for the state of the science (aphoristic vs methodic)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a science is still in growth, the aphoristic (collection of brief observations/maxims) treatment may be preferable to claims of a universal method; presenting an entire 'method' or perfect partitions too early misleads and arrests further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes early truth-seekers used aphorisms and did not pretend to a complete universal art; by contrast, modern pretensions to completeness ('methodum aspicias et partitiones, illae prorsus omnia complecti...') create a false appearance of perfection. Evaluate methodological claims relative to maturity of the field; penalize overconfident universal prescriptions and reward modest, empirical collections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intellectual vanity and artificially 'personated' sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition and affectation by those who present sciences as formally complete (using partitions and personations) deceive the popular intellect into thinking the science is whole when its 'members are poorly filled' (membra illa male impleta et veluti capsulae inanes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion flags rhetorical or formalistic presentations that mask substantive emptiness. Use it to judge whether a work's structure or jargon is serving to impress rather than to convey well-founded knowledge; encourage clarity, substance, and honest admission of limits.
